title: Diode I-V Curve: How Current Climbs Past the Knee
topic: Diode I-V characteristic — current is near zero below the knee voltage (~0.6 V for silicon), then climbs steeply once V_D crosses it; reverse bias passes only a tiny leakage current. A swept voltage slider drives a marker along the curve while a live current readout updates.

beats.narration: Turn the voltage on a diode up from zero — when does current finally start to flow?

elements.content: A diode doesn't pass current — until it does.

beats.narration: Put an adjustable source across a diode and measure the current. The diode is forward biased when V D is positive, anode to cathode.

elements.content: Adjustable voltage source on the left
V_D across the diode, I_D through the loop
anode → cathode is the forward direction

beats.narration: Plot the current against the voltage. Below the knee — about zero point six volts for silicon — almost no current flows. Cross the knee and the current climbs nearly exponentially.

elements.content: Shockley curve traced in: flat near zero, sharp rise past V_knee
below the knee — off. Past the knee — wide open.

beats.narration: Sweep the source voltage and watch the operating point slide. Reverse bias — current pinned at zero. Past the knee — current rockets up.

elements.content: Operating point dot Q slides along the curve as V_D varies
elements.note: Genuine motion — Q position is driven by a triangular V_D sweep

elements.content: Live readout: V_D and I_D in mono

beats.narration: For pencil-and-paper work, treat it as a switch: open below the knee, a tiny fixed drop above.

elements.content: Off below 0.6 V — short above 0.6 V (with a small drop)
the ideal-diode model is good enough for most circuits
